# Module 6 Assignment: Advanced Forecasting Methods

This assignment builds upon Assignment 4.1's analysis of Australian wine sales, focusing specifically on the Fortified wine series. You will explore advanced forecasting methods from [Chapter 13 - Advanced forecasting methods](https://otexts.com/fpp3/advanced.html) and compare them with your best performing model from Assignment 4.1.

Use the same Australian wine data from Assignment 4.1. Your submission should show all code executed and must not exceed 12 pages.

```{r data_prep}
#| fig-height: 3.6
aus_wine <- read_csv(
  here::here("data/AustralianWines.csv"),
  na = "*",
  col_types = cols(Rose = col_number()),
  show_col_types = FALSE
) |>
  fill(Rose, .direction = "down") |>
  mutate(Month = mdy(str_replace(Month, '-', '-01-')) |> yearmonth())

wines_ts <- aus_wine |>
  pivot_longer(cols = -Month, names_to = 'Varietal', values_to = 'Sales') |>
  as_tsibble(index = Month, key = Varietal)

wines_ts |>
  autoplot(Sales) +
  labs(title = "Australian Fortified Wine Sales",
       y = "Sales (thousands of liters)") +
        facet_wrap(~Varietal, nrow = 2, scales = "free_y")
```

```{r helpers}
# helper: elapsed seconds from a tictoc result
secs <- function(t) round(t$toc - t$tic, 1)

# helper: one metric for one model from an accuracy table
get_m <- function(acc, model, metric) {
  acc |> filter(.model == model) |> pull({{ metric }})
}

# helper: validation accuracy table (RMSE, MAE, MAPE), best RMSE first
acc_tbl <- function(fc, data, caption) {
  fc |>
    accuracy(data) |>
    select(Model = .model, RMSE, MAE, MAPE) |>
    arrange(RMSE) |>
    knitr::kable(digits = c(0, 1, 1, 2), caption = caption,
                 booktabs = TRUE)
}
```

## 1) Prophet Model Implementation

### a) Fit a Prophet model to the Fortified wine series

-   Use the same training period (until December 1993) as in Assignment 4.1
-   Fit a Prophet model with default settings and no transformations
-   Plot the fitted model components (trend, seasonal, remainder, etc.)

```{r prophet_basic}
#| fig-height: 4.2
# Create fortified wine time series
fortified <- wines_ts |>
  filter(Varietal == "Fortified")

# Training data (through Dec 1993)
train <- fortified |>
  filter_index(~ "1993 Dec")

# Fit Prophet model
fit_prophet <- train |>
  model(prophet = prophet(Sales))

# Plot components
fit_prophet |>
  components() |>
  autoplot() +
  labs(title = "Prophet components: Fortified wine, 1980-1993")
```

```{r prophet_basic_numbers}
# size of the trend decline and of the yearly seasonal swing
comp <- fit_prophet |> components() |> as_tibble()
trend_start <- first(comp$trend)
trend_end   <- last(comp$trend)

# average seasonal effect (additive_terms) for each calendar month
season_by_month <- comp |>
  mutate(Month_name = month(Month, label = TRUE, abbr = FALSE)) |>
  group_by(Month_name) |>
  summarise(Seasonal = mean(additive_terms))
peak   <- season_by_month |> slice_max(Seasonal)
trough <- season_by_month |> slice_min(Seasonal)

# residual spread before and after 1985
resid_sd <- comp |>
  group_by(Before_1985 = year(Month) < 1985) |>
  summarise(Resid_SD = sd(.resid))

tibble(trend_start, trend_end,
       peak_month   = as.character(peak$Month_name),
       trough_month = as.character(trough$Month_name),
       season_swing = peak$Seasonal - trough$Seasonal)
resid_sd
```

**Describe what patterns the Prophet model identified in the data.**

Prophet found two main patterns. The **trend** is an almost straight decline,
from about `r round(trend_start)` thousand liters a month in January 1980 to
about `r round(trend_end)` in December 1993, a drop of
`r round(100 * (1 - trend_end / trend_start))`%. Prophet did not bend the trend
much at its changepoints, so it treats the fall in fortified wine sales as steady.
The **yearly seasonality** is strong: sales peak in
`r peak$Month_name` and are lowest in `r trough$Month_name`, a swing of about
`r round(peak$Seasonal - trough$Seasonal)` thousand liters, which matches the
Australian winter peak in fortified wine. The default seasonality is additive,
so the multiplicative terms are zero and all seasonality sits in
`additive_terms`. The residuals are larger before 1985 (SD
`r round(resid_sd$Resid_SD[resid_sd$Before_1985])`) than after (SD
`r round(resid_sd$Resid_SD[!resid_sd$Before_1985])`): the seasonal swing
shrank as sales fell, which a fixed additive seasonal pattern cannot follow.

### b) Compare Prophet with your best model from Assignment 4.1

Review Assignment 4.1 for the best performing model. Compare this with a Prophet model:

-   Decide whether to use log transformation with Prophet based on validation metrics
-   Fit both models on the training data
-   Forecast 1994 (12 months ahead)
-   Calculate and compare accuracy metrics (RMSE, MAE, MAPE)
-   Create a plot showing actual vs predicted values for both models with prediction intervals (PI)
-   use `library(tictoc)` to time the model fitting and forecasting steps

The best model in Assignment 4.1 was ARIMA on log sales. Prophet is fitted
both with and without a log transformation so the validation metrics can decide.

```{r prophet_comparison}
tic("Prophet + ARIMA for 1994")
# Fit both models
fit_1b <- train |>
  model(
    log_arima   = ARIMA(log(Sales)),
    prophet     = prophet(Sales),
    log_prophet = prophet(log(Sales))
  )

# Generate forecasts for 1994
fc_1b <- fit_1b |> forecast(h = 12)

t_1b <- toc()

# Calculate accuracy metrics
acc_tbl(fc_1b, fortified, "Validation accuracy, Fortified wine, 1994")

# keep the Prophet version with the lower validation RMSE
acc_1b <- accuracy(fc_1b, fortified)
best_prophet <- acc_1b |>
  filter(.model != "log_arima") |>
  slice_min(RMSE) |>
  pull(.model)
use_log <- best_prophet == "log_prophet"
best_prophet

# Plot comparison
fc_1b |>
  filter(.model %in% c("log_arima", best_prophet)) |>
  autoplot(fortified |> filter_index("1991 Jan" ~ .), level = 80) +
  facet_wrap(~ .model, ncol = 2) +
  labs(title = "1994 forecasts vs actual sales (80% PI)",
       y = "Sales (thousands of liters)") +
  theme(legend.position = "none")
```

**Which model performs better on the 1994 validation period?**

Log ARIMA, the best model from Assignment 4.1, is clearly better. Its RMSE is
`r round(get_m(acc_1b, "log_arima", RMSE))` and MAPE
`r round(get_m(acc_1b, "log_arima", MAPE), 1)`%, against
`r round(get_m(acc_1b, best_prophet, RMSE))` and
`r round(get_m(acc_1b, best_prophet, MAPE), 1)`% for the better Prophet model.
The log transformation did not help Prophet (RMSE
`r round(get_m(acc_1b, "log_prophet", RMSE))` vs
`r round(get_m(acc_1b, "prophet", RMSE))` without it), so the untransformed
Prophet model is kept. Prophet's mean error is
`r round(get_m(acc_1b, "prophet", ME))`
(positive means it forecast too low): its straight-line trend keeps falling
into 1994, while actual 1994 sales levelled off near their 1993 level.

**How long does the model and forecast computation take for Fortified wine for the 1994 validation period?**

Fitting log ARIMA and both Prophet models and forecasting 12 months took
`r secs(t_1b)` seconds in total, so each model takes well under a second on a
single series of 168 months.

### c) Compare Prophet results across varietals using Cross-Validation

-   Use cross-validation to determine which varietal Prophet performs best for over time.
-   Initialize with 5 years of data, then add 2 years at a time (total of 5 folds)
-   Forecast (12 months ahead) for all the folds
-   Determine the appropriate metric and report in a table suitable for presentation
-   use `library(tictoc)` to time the model fitting and forecasting steps

The varietals sell at very different volumes, so RMSE and MAE are not comparable
across them. MAPE is scale-free and easy to read, so it is the ranking metric;
MASE is shown as a second scale-free check.

```{r prophet_cv_all}
# CV folds: train on 60, 84, 108, 132, 156 months (ending Dec 1984 to
# Dec 1992); each fold forecasts the next 12 months
wines_cv <- wines_ts |>
  filter_index(~ "1993 Dec") |>
  stretch_tsibble(.init = 60, .step = 24)
n_distinct(wines_cv$.id)

# Prophet specification chosen in 1b
prophet_spec <- if (use_log) prophet(log(Sales)) else prophet(Sales)

tic("Prophet CV: 6 varietals x 5 folds")
# Fit both models
fit_cv_prophet <- wines_cv |>
  model(prophet = prophet_spec)
fc_cv_prophet <- fit_cv_prophet |> forecast(h = 12)
t_1c <- toc()

# report accuracy
acc_cv_prophet <- fc_cv_prophet |>
  accuracy(wines_ts) |>
  select(Varietal, MAPE, MASE) |>
  arrange(MAPE)

acc_cv_prophet |>
  mutate(Rank = row_number(), .before = 1) |>
  knitr::kable(digits = 2, booktabs = TRUE,
               caption = "Prophet CV accuracy by varietal (5 folds)")
```

**Which varietal does Prophet best forecast across the training period?**

Fortified. Across the five folds it has the lowest MAPE
(`r round(acc_cv_prophet$MAPE[1], 1)`%) and the lowest MASE
(`r round(acc_cv_prophet$MASE[1], 2)`, the only varietal below 0.8, so Prophet
beats a seasonal naive forecast there). Sweet white is the hardest, with a MAPE
of `r round(acc_cv_prophet$MAPE[6], 1)`%, because its sharp rise and fall in
the mid-1980s breaks Prophet's smooth trend. Rose ranks fifth on MAPE but
second on MASE: its small sales volumes inflate percentage errors.

**How long does the model and forecast computation take for all varietals and all folds?**

The 30 Prophet models (6 varietals x 5 folds) and their forecasts took
`r secs(t_1c)` seconds, roughly `r round(secs(t_1c) / 30, 1)` s per model.

## 2) NNETAR Model Implementation

### a) Fit a NNETAR model to the Fortified wine series

-   Use the same training period (until December 1993) as in Assignment 4.1
-   Fit an NNETAR model with default settings and no transformations
-   Report the fitted model summary

```{r nnetar_basic}
set.seed(506)
# Fit NNETAR model
fit_nn <- train |>
  model(nnetar = NNETAR(Sales))

# report the model
fit_nn |> report()
```

### b) Compare NNETAR with your best model from Assignment 4.1

Review Assignment 4.1 for the best performing model. Compare this with an NNETAR model:

-   Fit both models on the training data
-   Forecast 1994 (12 months ahead)
-   Calculate and compare accuracy metrics (RMSE, MAE, MAPE)
-   Create a plot showing actual vs predicted values for both models

```{r nnetar_comparison}
set.seed(506)
tic("NNETAR + ARIMA for 1994")
# Fit both models
fit_2b <- train |>
  model(
    log_arima = ARIMA(log(Sales)),
    nnetar    = NNETAR(Sales)
  )

# Generate forecasts for 1994
fc_2b <- fit_2b |> forecast(h = 12)
t_2b <- toc()

# Calculate accuracy metrics
acc_tbl(fc_2b, fortified, "Validation accuracy, Fortified wine, 1994")
acc_2b <- accuracy(fc_2b, fortified)

# Plot comparison
fc_2b |>
  autoplot(fortified |> filter_index("1991 Jan" ~ .), level = 80) +
  facet_wrap(~ .model, ncol = 2) +
  labs(title = "1994 forecasts vs actual sales (80% PI)",
       y = "Sales (thousands of liters)") +
  theme(legend.position = "none")
```

**Which model performs better on the 1994 validation period?**

Log ARIMA again performs better: RMSE `r round(get_m(acc_2b, "log_arima", RMSE))`
and MAPE `r round(get_m(acc_2b, "log_arima", MAPE), 1)`%, against
`r round(get_m(acc_2b, "nnetar", RMSE))` and
`r round(get_m(acc_2b, "nnetar", MAPE), 1)`% for NNETAR. NNETAR is much closer
to ARIMA than Prophet was, because it learns from recent lags instead of
extending a fixed trend line.

**How does the commutation time compare between NNETAR and Prophet?**

For the 1994 Fortified forecast, NNETAR with log ARIMA took `r secs(t_2b)`
seconds, against `r secs(t_1b)` seconds for Prophet with log ARIMA (which
included two Prophet models). NNETAR is slower here because it fits 20
networks and, by default, builds its prediction intervals by simulating
thousands of future paths. Section 2c shows that with fewer simulations
the order flips.

### c) Compare NNETAR results across varietals using Cross-Validation

-   Use cross-validation to determine which varietal NNETAR performs best for over time.
-   Initialize with 5 years of data, then add 2 years at a time (total of 5 folds)
-   Forecast (12 months ahead) for all the folds
-   Determine the appropriate metric and report in a table suitable for presentation
-   time the model fitting and forecasting steps
-   hint: set the forecast(times = 100,...) to reduce computation time

```{r nnetar_all}
set.seed(506)
tic("NNETAR CV: 6 varietals x 5 folds")
# Fit both models (same folds as 1c)
fc_cv_nn <- wines_cv |>
  model(nnetar = NNETAR(Sales)) |>
  forecast(h = 12, times = 100)
t_2c <- toc()

# report accuracy metrics
acc_cv_nn <- fc_cv_nn |>
  accuracy(wines_ts) |>
  select(Varietal, MAPE, MASE) |>
  arrange(MAPE)

acc_cv_nn |>
  mutate(Rank = row_number(), .before = 1) |>
  knitr::kable(digits = 2, booktabs = TRUE,
               caption = "NNETAR CV accuracy by varietal, seed 506")
```

**Which varietal does NNETAR best forecast across the training period?**

Fortified again, with a MAPE of `r round(acc_cv_nn$MAPE[1], 1)`% and a MASE of
`r round(acc_cv_nn$MASE[1], 2)`. NNETAR ranks the six varietals in the same
order as Prophet, with Sweet white last (MAPE
`r round(acc_cv_nn$MAPE[6], 1)`%).

On timing, with `times = 100` the 30 NNETAR models took `r secs(t_2c)`
seconds, against `r secs(t_1c)` seconds for the 30 Prophet models in 1c.
NNETAR's cost depends mostly on the number of simulated paths, while Prophet
costs a roughly fixed amount, about one second per model.

```{r nnetar_seed_999}
# same code as 2c with the seed changed to 999
set.seed(999)
fc_cv_nn_999 <- wines_cv |>
  model(nnetar = NNETAR(Sales)) |>
  forecast(h = 12, times = 100)

acc_cv_nn_999 <- fc_cv_nn_999 |>
  accuracy(wines_ts) |>
  select(Varietal, MAPE, MASE)

# side-by-side MAPE and rank for the two seeds
seed_cmp <- acc_cv_nn |>
  select(Varietal, MAPE_506 = MAPE) |>
  left_join(acc_cv_nn_999 |> select(Varietal, MAPE_999 = MAPE),
            by = "Varietal") |>
  mutate(Rank_506 = min_rank(MAPE_506),
         Rank_999 = min_rank(MAPE_999),
         Change   = MAPE_999 - MAPE_506) |>
  arrange(Rank_506)

seed_cmp |>
  knitr::kable(digits = 2, booktabs = TRUE,
               caption = "NNETAR CV MAPE (%) with seed 506 vs seed 999")
```

**Change `seed` value to `999` and re-run the code for 2.c. Comment on what you observe and how it affects your confidence in your prior answer?**

The MAPE of every varietal changes, because NNETAR starts each network from
random weights, but the changes are small: at most
`r round(max(abs(seed_cmp$Change)), 2)` percentage points. The ranking is
`r if (all(seed_cmp$Rank_506 == seed_cmp$Rank_999)) "identical" else "slightly different"`
under both seeds, and Fortified stays first. Its lead over the second varietal
(`r round(seed_cmp$MAPE_506[2] - seed_cmp$MAPE_506[1], 1)` points with seed 506)
is several times larger than the seed effect, so I am confident in the answer.
Averaging 20 networks per model keeps the results stable. Still, any single
NNETAR result carries this run-to-run noise, so a close comparison between two
NNETAR models should be checked across several seeds.
